CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain and swelling following motor vehicle accident

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 50-year-old right-handed male presenting for second opinion regarding right index finger injury. Injury occurred in March 2026 when he was a passenger in a vehicle that was rear-ended multiple times, causing him to brace himself and hyperextend his right index finger. For approximately three months since the injury, he has experienced persistent pain, swelling, and functional limitation. Patient reports inability to make a fist and describes pain that is sometimes "unbearable," particularly with driving. He initially presented to an orthopedic practice where he was referred to occupational therapy and underwent MRI imaging revealing a flexor tendon tear. He was offered steroid injection but declined due to prior adverse reaction to dexamethasone. Subsequently, he was counseled that steroid injection might worsen the tear. He seeks this second opinion to clarify diagnosis and treatment options given that he is right-handed and relies on his dominant hand for his work as an X-ray technician.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Reports prior reaction to methylprednisolone (itching).

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension

MEDICATIONS
Blood pressure medication (specific agent not documented during visit)

ALLERGIES
Dexamethasone (causes heart rate elevation)
Methylprednisolone (causes itching)

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient is employed as an X-ray technician and is right-handed. Injury sustained as passenger in motor vehicle accident. Currently not enrolled in physical therapy.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy-appearing male in no acute distress. Regular rate and rhythm with 2+ radial pulse.
Right Hand: Swelling and bruising over volar surface of index finger. Palmar creases normal with slight diminishment at PIP crease compared to middle finger. Index finger rests in approximately 10 degrees of PIP flexion. Tenderness elicited with palpation. Mild numbness noted. Active range of motion significantly limited with DIP flexion reported as sensation of tearing. Active PIP flexion limited. Passive range of motion limited by pain and stiffness. Unable to make fist. Collateral ligaments intact. Extensor tendons intact.

RESULTS
MRI of right hand (April 2026): Focal soft tissue swelling over right index MCP joint; partial-thickness tear of right flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendon; fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around FDP and FDS tendons; radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of index MCP joint intact; MCP joint capsule intact; extensor tendons intact.
X-ray of right hand (four views, today): No bony abnormalities; joint congruency maintained throughout lesser digits; no concerning soft tissue shadows; no arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of right index finger with partial-thickness tear of the FDS tendon. The FDS is the less important of the two flexor tendons; the flexor digitorum profundus extending to the fingertip remains intact. Peritendinous scar tissue and inflammation are restricting flexor tendon excursion through the pulley system.

Plan:
1. Steroid injection: Administered betamethasone (Celestone) 1 cc with lidocaine 0.5 cc to address inflammation and pain. Dexamethasone avoided due to patient's prior heart rate elevation; methylprednisolone avoided due to prior itching reaction. Betamethasone selected for water-soluble formulation with low toxicity and high therapeutic benefit. Patient experienced significant painful reaction to needle insertion on first attempt, requiring needle withdrawal and reassurance. Second attempt successful with only scant bleeding from small palmar vein, controlled with local pressure and bandage. Patient reassured of no harm to finger.

2. Home care: Ice finger this evening and take ibuprofen. Expected pain improvement over 3-5 days with continued improvement over subsequent weeks.

3. Activity: Patient counseled that finger movement will not cause additional injury as extensors and collateral ligaments are intact. Splinting contraindicated as it prevents necessary active movement. Patient instructed to actively mobilize finger despite discomfort.

4. Physical/Occupational therapy: Outpatient therapy once weekly for six weeks with emphasis on active and passive range of motion exercises. Goal is full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions. Patient to coordinate with previous therapy provider if possible.

5. Follow-up: Possible repeat injection if needed based on response. Patient reassured that pain reduction will allow better participation in therapy and progressive functional recovery.
